readerTitle: Netflix raised a price 60%. Three months later, 800,000 subscribers were gone.
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Netflix 2011) + 실제 연구 (Kahneman & Tversky 1979) + 실제 규제 (프랑스 2024) + 가상 사례 (청소 서비스, 사무용품 공급)
insight: 가격 인상은 기존 고객에게 손실로 느껴진다. 시간, 이유, 가치, 빠져나갈 길로 그 손실을 줄인다.
misconception: 인상 폭만 작으면 문제없다. 조용히 바꾸면 아무도 모른다.

sources.text: Tversky & Kahneman (1992). Advances in Prospect Theory. J. of Risk and Uncertainty.
France, Arrêté du 16 avril 2024 (réduction de quantité, « shrinkflation »)

factChecks.note: Netflix 2011년 수치: 3분기 미국 구독자 약 80만 명 감소(24.59M → 23.79M, Q3 2011 주주서한). 주가는 7월 고점 약 $300에서 11월 약 $63까지 떨어졌습니다(약 -79%). 카드에는 "roughly 75%"로 보수적으로 적었습니다.
"손실은 이득보다 약 2배 크게 느껴진다"는 손실회피 계수 추정치(약 2–2.25)를 단순화한 표현입니다.
프랑스 슈링크플레이션 표시 의무는 2024년 7월 1일 시행된 법령 기준입니다. 다른 국가 사례로 바꿀 때는 따로 확인이 필요합니다.

cards.title: Netflix raised a price 60%. Three months later, 800,000 subscribers were gone.
body: Every growing company has to raise prices eventually. Few do it well.
Today: why a price increase hurts more than a price cut helps, and how to raise prices without a revolt.

image.label: Line chart dropping sharply
image.brief: 급락하는 라인 차트에 빨간 TV 아이콘. 실제 넷플릭스 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You need to raise your price.
body: You run a house-cleaning service with 300 regular clients at $120 a visit. Wages and supplies have gone up, and you need to charge $140.
How do you roll it out?

options.text: Move everyone to $140 next week with a short text message
options.feedback: Fast, but it's the most painful version. Clients get a surprise loss with no time to adjust and no reason why. Expect cancellations and angry replies.

options.text: New clients pay $140 now. Regular clients stay at $120 for 3 months, with notice and a clear reason
options.feedback: This is the standard playbook. New clients never knew the old price, and regulars get time, an explanation and a reward for staying.

options.text: Keep $120 but quietly shorten each visit
options.feedback: This is shrinkflation. It avoids an announcement, but clients who notice the skipped corners feel tricked, and that lasts longer than a price rise.

cards.title: Loss aversion
body: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky found that losses feel roughly **twice as strong** as gains of the same size. Losing $10 hurts more than finding $10 feels good.
To a current customer, a price increase isn't a new price. It's **losing a price they already had**. The same $20 a new customer happily pays can make a current customer furious.

image.label: Scale: −$5 outweighs +$5
image.brief: 저울 일러스트. 한쪽 "−$5"가 무겁게 내려가고 반대쪽 "+$5"는 가볍게 올라감.

cards.title: Netflix, July 2011.
body: Netflix split its $9.99 DVD-plus-streaming plan into two separate plans at $7.99 each. For people who wanted both, that meant **$15.98, a 60% jump**, announced in a short blog post.
In September it said DVDs would move to a separate service called Qwikster. It dropped that plan a few weeks later.
Netflix lost about 800,000 US subscribers that quarter. Its stock fell roughly 75% from its July peak within a few months.

cards.title: Then it learned to raise prices often, and gently.
body: Netflix has raised prices many times since. The pattern is usually the same: a modest step, announced in advance, paired with more content or a new plan, and rolled out to existing members gradually.
Subscribers kept growing through most of those increases. The size of the increase matters, but **how it's delivered** matters at least as much.

image.label: Small steps up, line keeps rising
image.brief: 작은 계단식 가격 상승 그래프와 그 위로 꾸준히 오르는 구독자 곡선을 겹쳐서.

cards.title: Five rules for raising prices.
list: **Give notice.** 30 to 90 days, so it's a plan, not a surprise.
**Explain why** in the customer's terms: what they get, not what you need.
**Pair it with value**, such as a new feature, better support or more content.
**Protect loyalty.** Delay the increase for current customers, or let them lock in a yearly plan at the old price.
**Offer a way down.** A cheaper plan keeps people who would otherwise cancel.

cards.title: Shrinkflation is a price increase too.
body: Making a product smaller or weaker at the same price avoids the announcement. Customers notice eventually, and it feels like being tricked rather than charged more.
Regulators are noticing too. Since July 2024, France has required large supermarkets to label products whose quantity shrank while the price stayed the same or went up.

cards.title: Your business clients renew in 3 months.
body: You supply cleaning products to offices on yearly contracts. You're raising prices by 15%. When and how do you tell them?

options.feedback: They find out when the bill arrives. That's the surprise loss that sends buyers looking for another supplier.

options.text: 60–90 days ahead, with an option to renew early at today's price
options.feedback: Notice plus a reward for loyalty. Some clients renew early, which brings cash in sooner, and nobody is surprised.

options.text: Don't announce it. Most won't notice
options.feedback: Purchasing teams check invoices. The ones who notice will lose trust in you, and a price change without the notice your contract requires can break it.

cards.title: A price increase is a message. Deliver it like one.
body: Customers feel a loss about twice as hard as a gain. Your job is to soften it with time, a reason, added value and a way out.
**Try it today:** if you had to raise prices 20% next quarter, write the first two sentences of the email to your customers.
